conditions.label: S-posture
conditions.consequence: An exaggerated low-back arch at address pre-tensions the lower back and makes it harder to turn the pelvis without the spine taking the load.
conditions.injuryNote: A sustained end-range low-back arch under rotational load is associated with lower back discomfort. Worth raising with a clinician if pain is present.

conditions.label: C-posture
conditions.consequence: A rounded upper back at address reduces the thoracic rotation available, so the backswing turn is shorter and is usually made up for elsewhere.

conditions.label: Standing too upright
conditions.consequence: Too little forward bend from the hips leaves the arms no room to hang, so the swing tends to become flatter and more around the body.

conditions.label: Shoulders open at address
conditions.consequence: An open shoulder line at address points the swing left of the target line before the club has moved.

conditions.label: Shoulders closed at address
conditions.consequence: A closed shoulder line at address points the swing right of the target line before the club has moved.

conditions.label: Ball too far forward
conditions.consequence: A ball played too far toward the lead foot is met after the low point, which tends to open the shoulders at address to compensate.

conditions.label: Ball too far back
conditions.consequence: A ball played too far toward the trail foot is met early and steeply, which tends to close the shoulders at address to compensate.

conditions.label: Stance too wide
conditions.consequence: A wide base resists rotation, so the body tends to move laterally instead of turning.

conditions.label: Stance too narrow
conditions.consequence: A narrow base turns easily but gives less to push against and less lateral stability through impact.

conditions.label: Ball too close to the body
conditions.consequence: Standing too close crowds the arms and steepens the swing.

conditions.label: Ball too far from the body
conditions.consequence: Reaching for the ball pulls the shoulders forward and rounds the upper back, even in someone whose standing posture is fine.

conditions.label: Loss of posture
conditions.consequence: Losing the address spine angle during the swing changes the distance to the ball mid-swing, so the low point has to be found by compensation rather than by repetition.

conditions.label: Early extension
conditions.consequence: The pelvis moving toward the ball in the downswing takes away the room the arms need, leaving the hands to rescue the strike.

conditions.label: Reverse spine angle
conditions.consequence: Leaning toward the target at the top loads the trail side of the lower back and makes a sequenced downswing hard to start from the ground.
conditions.injuryNote: Combined end-range extension and rotation is the loading pattern most often linked with lower back pain in golfers. Worth raising with a clinician if pain is present.

conditions.label: Flat shoulder plane
conditions.consequence: Shoulders turning too horizontally at the top set the club behind the body, which is commonly recovered by throwing the upper body out at the start of the downswing.

conditions.label: Trail hip hike
conditions.consequence: The trail hip rising rather than rotating substitutes a vertical move for a turn and shortens the effective backswing.

conditions.label: Sway
conditions.consequence: Sliding away from the target in the backswing moves the low point behind the ball and has to be reversed exactly to strike it.

conditions.label: Slide
conditions.consequence: Excess lateral movement toward the target in the downswing outruns the rotation and leaves the face open at impact.

conditions.label: Hanging back
conditions.consequence: Weight left on the trail side at impact moves the low point behind the ball, costing compression and adding loft.

conditions.label: Forward lunge
conditions.consequence: The upper body moving toward the target ahead of the sequence steepens the attack and narrows the margin for a clean strike.

conditions.label: Late lead-knee buckle
conditions.consequence: A lead knee collapsing through impact drops the whole body and makes the strike depend on timing.

conditions.label: Flying trail elbow
conditions.consequence: A trail elbow lifted away from the body at the top disconnects the arms from the turn and requires a re-route to deliver the club.

conditions.label: Chicken wing
conditions.consequence: The lead arm folding through impact shortens the radius exactly where it should be longest, costing speed and consistency of face angle.

conditions.label: Over the top
conditions.consequence: The club moving outside the ideal path at the start of the downswing produces an out-to-in strike — a pull or a slice depending on the face.

conditions.label: Loss of width
conditions.consequence: The hands collapsing toward the chest in the backswing shortens the arc and removes the space the downswing needs to build speed.

conditions.label: Casting
conditions.consequence: Releasing the wrist angle early spends the stored angle before it can be used, so speed peaks before the ball rather than at it.

conditions.label: Scooping
conditions.consequence: Adding loft through impact with the lead wrist means the club is rising at the ball, costing compression and distance control.

conditions.label: Insufficient wrist set
conditions.consequence: Too little wrist angle by the top leaves less stored angle to release, so speed has to come from the body alone.

conditions.label: Out-of-order sequence
conditions.consequence: When the chest leads the pelvis, the chain that multiplies speed from the ground up never forms and speed has to be made by the arms.

conditions.label: Low separation
conditions.consequence: Little separation between the chest and the pelvis at the top means little elastic load to release, so the downswing starts from a standstill.

conditions.label: Rushed transition
conditions.consequence: Starting down too quickly relative to the backswing leaves the sequence no time to form from the ground up.

conditions.label: Limited trail-hip internal rotation
conditions.consequence: The pelvis turns away from the target over a planted trail foot, which requires the trail femur to rotate internally. When it cannot, the turn has to be found elsewhere.
conditions.injuryNote: Rotation that the hips cannot supply is usually taken from the lower back, which has very little rotation available. Worth raising with a clinician if pain is present.

conditions.label: Limited lead-hip internal rotation
conditions.consequence: The downswing turns the pelvis toward the target over the lead foot, to end range and quickly. A restriction here is the more common and more consequential of the two sides, and forces the pelvis to move rather than turn.
conditions.injuryNote: Rotation that the hips cannot supply is usually taken from the lower back, which has very little rotation available. Worth raising with a clinician if pain is present.

conditions.label: Poor pelvic disassociation
conditions.consequence: When the pelvis cannot move independently of the chest, the two turn together and no separation can be built or released.

conditions.label: Limited thoracic rotation
conditions.consequence: The upper back supplies most of the turn. When it is restricted the shoulders find their range by tilting or by taking it from the lower back.

conditions.label: Limited thoracic extension
conditions.consequence: An upper back that cannot straighten holds the golfer in flexion at address.

conditions.label: Fixed thoracic kyphosis
conditions.consequence: A structurally rounded upper back with tight chest and lat tissue and weak scapular retractors. Present standing upright, not only over the ball — which is what distinguishes it from a setup that merely reaches for the ball.

conditions.label: Limited shoulder flexion
conditions.consequence: Restricted overhead reach limits how wide the arms can travel.

conditions.label: Limited trail-shoulder external rotation
conditions.consequence: The trail arm needs external rotation to fold under the club at the top; without it the elbow lifts away instead.

conditions.label: Limited ankle dorsiflexion
conditions.consequence: Restricted ankles reduce how much the golfer can stay in their posture while the pelvis rotates.

conditions.label: Limited hip extension
conditions.consequence: Short hip flexors hold the pelvis in a forward tilt, which sets the low-back arch at address before the golfer has done anything.

conditions.label: Limited wrist mobility
conditions.consequence: Restricted wrists limit how much angle can be set and held.

conditions.label: Poor core stability
conditions.consequence: Without a stable middle, the posture set at address is not held under the loads of the swing.

conditions.label: Poor single-leg balance
conditions.consequence: The downswing is balanced over one leg. When that is difficult, the golfer widens the base or avoids moving onto the lead side at all.

conditions.label: Club too short for the golfer
conditions.consequence: A club that is short for the golfer makes them reach down and forward for the ball. Club length is measured; fitting it to the golfer needs a reference this product does not capture.

conditions.label: Trying to lift the ball
conditions.consequence: An intent to help the ball into the air produces the opposite of the motion that does.

conditions.label: Aims left of the target
conditions.consequence: A perceptual bias that sets the body left of where the golfer believes it is.

conditions.label: Aims right of the target
conditions.consequence: A perceptual bias that sets the body right of where the golfer believes it is.

conditions.label: Settled tempo habit
conditions.consequence: A habitual rhythm carried between shots and clubs.

conditions.label: Settled setup preference
conditions.consequence: A stance width the golfer has settled on and repeats without thinking about it.
